part_title: Database Selection Guide and Integrated GenAI Data Architecture

scenes.title: Choosing a database by access pattern
scenes.narration: The slide compares four distinct access patterns. Neptune is the graph-oriented choice when the question asks for relationships or multi-hop connections. A vector search system is appropriate when the problem is semantic similarity across documents, images or other embedded content. ElastiCache or MemoryDB suits fast access to sessions, counters, reusable results or other in-memory structures, with durability requirements determining which is appropriate. DocumentDB serves flexible nested JSON documents and evolving application metadata. Read the example questions rather than choosing from brand names. “What is connected to this entity?” suggests graph traversal. “Which passages resemble this question?” suggests embeddings and vector search. “What is the latest session state?” suggests a low-latency key-based lookup. “How do I store evolving customer profiles?” suggests a document model. Real GenAI workflows can need several stores simultaneously. Design the consistency, security, cost and retrieval path for each. A vector store doesn't automatically validate a factual claim, and a graph database doesn't replace transactional data controls.

scenes.title: Integrated GenAI database architecture
scenes.narration: The closing architecture places purpose-built data stores behind a GenAI orchestrator. On the left are transactional records, enterprise documents, business applications and streaming events. Ingestion and enrichment processes prepare this information for different storage needs. The middle layer includes operational databases, a low-latency cache for session or intermediate data, Neptune for connected facts and a vector index in a supported search or database engine for semantic retrieval. When a user asks a question, the orchestrator identifies the required evidence, retrieves from one or more authorised stores, combines the results and invokes Amazon Bedrock. The answer includes citations so the user can trace its supporting sources. Follow the feedback loop at the bottom: new documents, user interactions and evaluated outcomes update the governed data and retrieval processes. This is not permission to expose all sources to every request. Each branch needs tenant and role-aware filters, freshness checks and provenance. The important architectural lesson is to assign storage technology by query semantics while coordinating them through one secure, observable answering pipeline.
